# Terman's Garden: The Research Park {#sec-4-01}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1945–1955
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does a university become an operating system for an
economy?

**The answer.** By becoming a landlord. Stanford could not sell the eight
thousand acres the Founding Grant gave it, so Terman leased them — and in doing
so made the university simultaneously the landlord, the talent supply, the
research partner, and the legitimacy anchor of the companies on its own land. A
constraint in an 1885 legal document produced the business model of the
twentieth century.

**The mechanism.** All three, fused into one institution and one balance sheet.
The Research Park is the moment the university stops mediating other people's
power and starts holding its own: rent from the land, credentials for the
workforce, research contracts from the state, and equity in the outcomes.

**The key fact.** The Founding Grant prohibited selling the land. That
prohibition — a clause written by a grieving railroad baron to protect his
memorial — is why Stanford leases rather than sells, and therefore why it
captured the appreciation of the most valuable industrial real estate on earth.

**The human anchor.** Terman as landlord and dean at once, deciding which
companies get to be neighbours. The most consequential zoning authority in
American economic history.

**Excluded voices.** Palo Alto and the surrounding towns, whose housing markets
and restrictive covenants determined who could live near the jobs. The Research
Park's labour force was filtered by residential exclusion before it was filtered
by hiring.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the university became the operating system
of a regional economy by showing it simultaneously occupy the roles of landlord,
credentialler, research partner, and legitimacy source for the firms on its
land.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

The Founding Grant of 1885 forbade Stanford from selling its land. A grieving
railroad baron wrote that clause to protect his son's memorial from future
trustees, and sixty-six years later it produced the business model of the
twentieth century — because a university that cannot sell land can still lease
it.

The Stanford Industrial Park opened in 1951, the first university-owned
industrial park in the United States, with Varian as its first tenant and
Hewlett-Packard arriving in 1956. Page Mill Road became its spine. What made it
more than a property development was that the university now occupied four
positions at once with respect to the companies on its land. It was their
landlord. It was their talent supply. It was their research partner. And it was
their legitimacy anchor, because a company adjacent to Stanford was a company
that federal agencies and private investors took seriously.

No other institution in the country held all four. That combination is what the
chapter means by calling the university an operating system for a regional
economy.

Terman extended it through the Honors Cooperative Program in 1954, which let
engineers at local companies take graduate courses part-time while employed. The
university thereby became a continuously running industrial utility rather than
a place people left at twenty-two, and the firms became permanently entangled
with the institution that credentialed their staff.

The chapter follows the revenue honestly. Much of the park's early tenancy
depended on defence contracts, which means the private-sector face of the
arrangement sat on a public-sector income stream — Act III's triangle with a
lease attached.

Who could take the jobs was determined before hiring began. Palo Alto and the
surrounding towns operated restrictive covenants and exclusionary practices that
filtered the residential population within reach of the park, and the chapter
names them specifically.

The operating system is running. Everything else in Act IV is an application
built on top of it.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does a university become an operating system for an economy?
:::

The Founding Grant of 1885 forbids the university to sell its land.

Leland Stanford wrote that clause, or had it written, to protect his son's
memorial from future trustees who might liquidate it. It is a grieving father's
provision, and for sixty-six years it functioned exactly as a dead hand
provision usually does: it locked up an asset and prevented anyone from doing
anything useful with it.

Then somebody noticed that a university which cannot sell land can still lease
it.

## The problem, restated as an opportunity

By the late 1940s Stanford had eight thousand acres of the San Francisco
Peninsula and a chronic shortage of money. The endowment was adequate rather
than large. The land was used for grazing, agriculture, and a golf course, and
generated very little.

Terman and the university's business manager, Alf Brandin, worked out the
implications. Long-term ground leases would produce income without violating the
Grant. And the tenants could be chosen.

That last point is the one that matters, and it is why this is a chapter about
power rather than about real estate. A landlord who selects tenants on the basis
of strategic fit rather than rent is exercising industrial policy over a region.

## 1951

The Stanford Industrial Park — later the Research Park — opened in 1951 along
Page Mill Road, the first university-owned industrial park in the United States.
Varian Associates was the first tenant, for the reasons the previous act
described: it was founded by Stanford researchers on Stanford technology, and it
was already entangled with the institution.

Eastman Kodak took space. General Electric came. Hewlett-Packard moved from its
various rented premises to the park in 1956 and stayed, which meant the company
that had started in the garage at 367 Addison Avenue became a tenant of the
university whose professor had told it to stay in California.

The leases were long — fifty-one years and then ninety-nine — and the terms
included restrictions on what could be built and who could occupy it. The
university was not merely collecting rent. It was zoning.

## Four roles at once

Here is what makes the arrangement different in kind from any other university-
industry relationship then in existence. Stanford occupied four distinct
positions with respect to the firms on its land, simultaneously.

It was their **landlord**, on long leases at terms it set, on land it could not
sell and therefore had no incentive to develop for any other purpose.

It was their **talent supply**, producing the engineers they hired and, through
the Honors Cooperative Program from 1954, continuing to educate those engineers
after they were hired. Employees of member companies could take graduate courses
part-time, with their employers paying the fees. A university that educates a
company's staff for the duration of their careers is not a supplier; it is
infrastructure.

It was their **research partner**, through sponsored research, consulting
relationships, and faculty who sat on their boards or founded them.

And it was their **legitimacy anchor**. A young company on Stanford land,
staffed by Stanford graduates, doing work adjacent to Stanford research, was
legible to federal contracting officers and to investors in a way that an
identical company in an industrial district thirty miles away was not.

No other institution in the country held all four. That combination is what the
chapter means in calling the university an operating system for a regional
economy: not a metaphor about influence, but a literal description of an entity
supplying the land, the labour, the research, and the credentialling for an
industry growing on top of it.

## Follow the revenue

The park's early tenants were not consumer companies and the chapter should keep
Act III's substrate visible.

Varian made klystrons and microwave equipment, and its customers were military.
Hewlett-Packard's instrument business depended heavily on defence and aerospace
purchasing. Lockheed's missile division would arrive in Sunnyvale in 1956, and
Act IV chapter 4 is about what that did to the region.

The private-sector face of the arrangement sat on a public-sector income stream.
Federal procurement paid for most of it, and the park was the mechanism by which
that money became a real estate portfolio, a graduate programme, and a set of
private fortunes.

## Steeples, tenants, and the loop

The strategy from Act III chapter 10 now closes into a circuit, and it is worth
tracing once because the rest of the act assumes it.

Federal money funds research in the fields Terman selected. The research
produces technology and trained people. Faculty and graduates found companies to
commercialise it. The companies lease land in the park, which pays the
university. Their employees enrol in the cooperative programme, which pays the
university. Their research needs sponsor further work, which pays the university
and generates the next technology. Their success attracts the next generation of
students and faculty, which strengthens the steeples, which attracts more
federal money.

Every stage of that loop feeds the next, and the university takes a position at
every stage.

Terman became provost in 1955 and ran the university's academic strategy for a
decade. The industrial park expanded. By the mid-1960s the region had a name for
itself as a technology centre, and by 1971 a trade journalist had supplied the
label that stuck.

## The other university

There is a comparison that clarifies what Stanford actually did, and it is
thirty miles north.

Berkeley in 1951 was the stronger institution by most measures. It had the
Radiation Laboratory, the Manhattan Project pedigree, more Nobel laureates, and
larger federal research funding. If you had been asked in 1951 which Bay Area
university would anchor a technology industry, the answer would have been
obvious and wrong.

Berkeley did not build an industrial park, and could not have. It is a public
university, embedded in a city, on a constrained site, governed by regents
appointed through a political process and accountable to a state legislature. It
could not have leased public land to private companies on preferential terms
without a fight it would have lost, and its faculty consulting and spin-out
arrangements were more restricted.

Stanford was private, governed by a self-perpetuating board answerable to
nobody, and sitting on eight thousand contiguous acres that could not be sold
and therefore had to be used.

The Founding Grant's insulation from politics, written in 1885 to protect a
memorial, turned out sixty-six years later to be the decisive competitive
advantage in a business nobody had imagined. Berkeley did the better science for
decades and Stanford captured the industry, and the difference is a governance
structure.

## Who could live there

The workforce for all this had to live somewhere, and where it could live had
been determined before any of it was built.

Palo Alto, Menlo Park, Atherton, and the surrounding towns operated restrictive
covenants of the kind described in Act III, and the federal underwriting maps
graded the area accordingly. The covenants became judicially unenforceable in
1948 but remained in deeds and continued to be honoured informally, and the
practices of local real estate boards and lenders sustained the pattern for
decades afterwards.

The best-documented local case is the developer Joseph Eichler, who from the
early 1950s built subdivisions on the Peninsula and refused to discriminate,
selling to Black and Asian buyers when almost nobody else in the region would.
He resigned from the National Association of Home Builders over its refusal to
adopt a non-discrimination policy. His developments were exceptional, and their
being exceptional is the evidence.

East Palo Alto, immediately across the freeway from the university and the park,
became substantially Black in the same decades, with a very different tax base,
different schools, and no access to the housing appreciation happening a mile
away.

The industrial park's labour force was filtered by residence before it was
filtered by hiring. That is not incidental to the story of Silicon Valley's
prosperity. It is a condition of it, and the boundary is still visible from the
road.

## The operating system is running

By 1955 the machine has been assembled and switched on. Everything in the rest
of this act is an application built on top of it: semiconductors, then personal
computers, then the internet, then platforms, then models.

The first application arrives the following year, when a Nobel laureate moves to
Mountain View to be near his mother.
